Krichene and Rendle show that sampled ranking metrics can reverse model orderings relative to full-catalog metrics, even in expectation. Fixing the 99 negative candidates supports consistent paired comparisons, but does not remove sampling bias. Report results as HR@10 under the pinned sampled-candidate protocol; improvements do not establish better full-catalog recommendation. Keep the host evaluator unchanged. [On Sampled Metrics for Item Recommendation](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

For this benchmark, a suitable uncertainty analysis is a paired, dataset-stratified user bootstrap: retain each user’s hit indicators across all fusion settings, resample 200 users with replacement within each category using identical sampled indices for every setting, then recompute the four-category macro-average and its difference from baseline. Report the observed difference, a bootstrap interval, per-category results, and discordant-user counts. One changed hit moves a category’s HR by 0.5 percentage points and the macro-average by 0.125 points. These intervals describe user-sampling uncertainty conditional on the four datasets, trained models, and fixed candidates; they exclude training-seed and candidate-resampling variability. This is a methodological recommendation for the stated design.

Repeatedly choosing the best fusion setting on the same validation users risks selection overfitting: the winning score is optimistic, and an ordinary bootstrap interval computed after selection does not correct that optimism. Cawley and Talbot show that selection bias can rival differences between algorithms. Limit and disclose the search, treat small gains as exploratory, and freeze the selected configuration before independent held-out evaluation. [On Over-fitting in Model Selection](https://www.jmlr.org/beta/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)
